nameStory: The red buckeye gets its name from its brilliant red, tubular flowers that earned it the nickname 'firecracker plant' - they really do look like tiny red fireworks exploding from the branch tips! The 'buckeye' part comes from the large, glossy brown seeds that have a lighter patch resembling the eye of a male deer (a buck).
description: Red buckeye is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that typically grows 10-20 feet tall, making it one of the more compact members of the buckeye family. It's famous for its show-stopping clusters of bright red, tubular flowers that bloom in spring before many other trees leaf out. This southern native has found a home in New England gardens and occasional naturalized spots, where its early spring color display makes it a real attention-grabber.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright red, tubular flowers cluster at branch tips in upright spikes 4-6 inches long, blooming in late spring. Each individual flower is about an inch long with protruding red stamens that give the cluster a fuzzy, bottlebrush appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Hand-shaped leaves with 5 leaflets radiating from a central point like fingers on a palm. The leaflets feel smooth and are arranged opposite each other on the branches, creating a very symmetrical look.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, glossy brown seeds (buckeyes) about an inch across with a prominent light-colored scar that really does look like an eye. They're contained in smooth capsules that split open in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small, rounded tree or large multi-stemmed shrub, usually staying under 20 feet tall. The branching pattern is very regular and symmetrical, giving it a neat, organized appearance even in winter.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, sticky winter buds that feel tacky to the touch and are arranged opposite each other on the branches. They're reddish-brown and quite noticeable against bare winter branches.

habitat: In New England, red buckeye is primarily found in cultivated settings like botanical gardens, arboretums, and residential landscapes where it's been planted as an ornamental. Occasionally it may naturalize in woodland edges or disturbed areas with rich, well-drained soil, particularly in warmer microclimates.

seasonality.spring: The spectacular red flower clusters bloom in late spring, usually May, creating the most dramatic identification opportunity of the year. New leaves emerge around the same time, showing their distinctive hand-shaped pattern.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with the characteristic five-leaflet palmate leaves, though less showy than during flowering. Small green seed capsules begin developing if flowers were pollinated by hummingbirds or butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to yellow-brown before dropping, and the large, glossy brown buckeye seeds are released from their splitting capsules. The distinctive seeds scattered on the ground are a sure sign this tree is nearby.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the symmetrical branching pattern and large, sticky, opposite buds that are diagnostic of the buckeye family. The neat, rounded crown shape is still apparent.

funFact: Red buckeye is one of the few trees that can successfully grow and bloom in Finland, despite being native to the warm southeastern United States - it's so hardy that it thrives 1,000 miles north of where it naturally occurs!
confusionNotes: The red flowers make this hard to confuse with anything else when blooming, but the hand-shaped leaves might be mistaken for red maple. Remember: red buckeye has 5 leaflets per leaf arranged like fingers, while red maple has one leaf blade with 3-5 lobes - buckeye leaves can be pulled apart into separate pieces, maple leaves cannot.
contextualKnowledge: Like all buckeyes, the seeds and other parts of red buckeye are toxic to humans and most animals if eaten, despite their attractive appearance. Native Americans traditionally used buckeye seeds in folk remedies, but this should never be attempted without expert knowledge.
compareHints: Red buckeye is easily distinguished from other buckeyes by its bright red flowers - horse-chestnut has white flowers, Ohio buckeye has yellowish-green flowers, and yellow buckeye has yellow flowers. It's also the smallest of the buckeyes commonly grown in New England, staying more shrub-like while others become larger trees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horse-chestnut is the only member of the Aesculus genus commonly found as a large tree in New England, making it fairly easy to distinguish from its relatives.
Unlike its tree-form relatives like horse-chestnut and Ohio buckeye, bottlebrush buckeye stays shrub-sized and spreads by suckers rather than growing as a single trunk.
